query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloy, local structural disorder (e.g., defects, strain, and compositional inhomogeneities) leads to a broad distribution of magnetic exchange interactions that govern both the sharpness and hysteresis of the magnetocaloric response during low‐applied-field cycles. Reducing these defects via a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment will homogenize the exchange interactions, thereby reducing hysteretic losses and modifying the entropy change profile.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high‐entropy alloy with a high density of microstructural defects and an inhomogeneous magnetic exchange landscape.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment at a temperature sufficiently high to relieve residual stresses and reduce defect density but below the recrystallization threshold, under an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Annealing at a defined temperature (controlled variable; e.g., T_anneal well below melting/recrystallization) for a specified time, followed by magnetic refrigeration cycle tests under low-applied-field conditions over the magnetostructural transition temperature range.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced density of defects and more homogeneous lattice strain, leading to a narrower distribution of magnetic exchange parameters.
generation.mechanism: The annealing process diminishes microstructural inhomogeneities, thereby narrowing the spread in exchange interactions. This 'homogenization' minimizes pinning effects that contribute to hysteresis and sharpens the magnetocaloric entropy change profile, potentially broadening the effective working temperature range and reducing energy losses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline as‐deposited alloy, the annealed sample will exhibit a measurable reduction in magnetic hysteresis (i.e., lower coercivity in M–H loops) and a modified (less sharp and possibly slightly broadened) magnetic entropy change vs. temperature curve under low field cycling. The primary measured property (magnetic entropy change) will shift to display reduced hysteretic losses.
generation.baseline: The as‐deposited state, characterized by a high level of defects and a broad, hysteretic magnetocaloric response with a sharp entropy change peak.
generation.boundary: This prediction applies under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles conducted over the operating temperature range characteristic of the magnetostructural transition in the FeMnNiGeSi alloy, and for samples processed with comparable compositions and cooling histories.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative changes in hysteresis width and the entropy change magnitude are uncertain; slight variations in the annealing temperature, time, or residual compositional inhomogeneity may affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group remains in the as-deposited state, and the other group undergoes the controlled low-temperature annealing treatment. Characterize both sets using microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM, XRD) to verify differences in defect density, then perform magnetocaloric tests (measuring ΔS(T) curves and M–H hysteresis loops) under identical low-applied-field conditions.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) vs. temperature curves
Coercivity and hysteresis losses from M–H loops
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis (coercivity) and a discernible modification of the ΔS(T) profile (in agreement with a lower defect density) compared to the as-deposited baseline, then the hypothesis—that microstructural disorder governs the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Changes in −ΔSmax as well as the changes in the shape of the −ΔS(ΔH, T) curves are important to MCE when applied to magnetic refrigeration, as they may lead to changes in the overall refrigerant capacity (RC). RC in general is the figure of merit used to compare MCE materials giving the total heat transfer of the material over a typical refrigeration cycle. RC for a given ΔH is calculated as the integral of −ΔS(T) over a temperature range of interest: Here, TR1 and TR2 are traditionally taken to be the temperatures corresponding to the FWHM of the −ΔS(T) feature on the low and high temperature sides of the peak, respectively. We do not consider hysteretic losses here, as the M(H) loops showed negligible hysteresis, though that can be important in many systems. Figure 5 shows RC as a function of ΔH for both the annealed and as-rolled samples. The RC of 36 J/kg for a 1 T field change puts these HEAs below many other materials designed to operate in the 100–200 K range, though several factors related to pragmatic engineering issues (e.g., ductility, corrosion resistance, high thermal conductivity) may make up for this.
